issues.legal_issue: A partition does not defeat a creditor’s claim against a son’s share when the son fails to establish that the partition made adequate provision for the father’s debts.
material_facts: A father and his minor son were members of an undivided Hindu family that owned property in more than one state.
After the father incurred debts, a partition deed divided only the family’s property in one state into equal shares and assigned the father responsibility for certain debts.
The father had numerous other debts, and the partition did not provide for all of them.
The son did not establish the value of the property available to the father or that his allotted share was adequate to discharge the debts.
The creditor sought to enforce its security against the son’s share.
issues.conclusion: The partition was not binding on the creditor. The son bore the burden of establishing that the arrangement made proper and adequate provision for the debts; that burden was not met.
issues.legal_principle: Under Panna Lal v. Mst. Naraini, a son may remain liable after partition for the father’s pre-partition debts that are not illegal or immoral if no proper arrangement for their payment was made at partition. Whether an arrangement is adequate depends on the circumstances. The son who relies on the partition to discharge his liability must establish that the arrangement made proper and adequate provision. A partition need not be fraudulent to fail to bind a creditor if it makes no adequate provision for the debts.

issues.definition: When a creditor seeks a son’s allotted property for the father’s pre-partition debts, a partition that lacks adequate provision for all those debts and whose adequacy the son fails to establish does not bind the creditor.

issues.legal_issue: The law governing a Hindu owner’s authority to mortgage joint family property is the owner’s personal law, not the law of the place where the property is situated merely because it is located there.
material_facts: The father and his family were permanent residents and domiciled in one state, while the mortgaged family property was in another state.
The dispute concerned whether the father’s mortgage of joint family property bound his son.
The law applied in the state where the property was situated differed from the Hindu law governing the family’s domicile.
issues.conclusion: The law of the family’s domicile governed the father’s authority to mortgage the property; the law of the property’s situs did not apply merely because the land was situated there.
issues.legal_principle: The power to dispose of or encumber property depends on the owner’s personal law, as modified by applicable legislation, rather than on an assumed lex situs that operates irrespective of personal law. Hindu law is personal law and forms part of the status of a family governed by it. The Court applied the principles set out in Brij Narain v. Mangal Prasad, as approved in Panna Lal v. Mst. Naraini, and referred to Mayne’s Hindu Law. It also noted that Chidambara Mudaliar v. Kootha Perumal had been overruled by the Full Bench in Venkataramayya v. Venkataramana.

issues.legal_issue: A father’s mortgage of joint family property for a personal debt binds his son’s interest to the extent the mortgage secures a debt that was antecedent in fact and time and independent of the mortgage transaction.
material_facts: The father borrowed money for a new personal business that was not a family necessity or benefit, and the borrowing was not illegal or immoral.
Before the mortgage was created, the father owed the same bank substantial amounts on two overdraft accounts.
The bank handed the father a new loan by a separate draft while the earlier overdraft debts remained outstanding and unsecured.
The father deposited the draft into an overdraft account, and the earlier debts were thereby discharged.
The family was undivided when the mortgage was created; the later partition did not establish a defence to the creditor’s security.
The Court found that the entire new loan was used to discharge the pre-existing debts and that the transactions were factually dissociated.
issues.conclusion: The prior overdraft indebtedness was antecedent in fact and time, notwithstanding that the same bank was the creditor and the new loan was used to pay the earlier debts. The mortgage therefore bound the son’s share to the extent of the loan secured by it, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Brij Narain v. Mangal Prasad, approved and adopted in Panna Lal v. Mst. Naraini, a father may, while the family remains undivided, alienate joint family property to discharge antecedent personal debts that are not illegal or immoral. A mortgage for a debt incurred at the same time is not binding on the son merely as a mortgage unless it discharges an antecedent debt. Antecedence requires both time and fact: the prior debt must be truly independent of the mortgage debt, and the transactions must be dissociated in fact. Whether that separation exists depends on the nature of the transactions, the parties’ intention, and the form in which they carried out the transaction. The Court also referred to Chidambara Mudaliar v. Kootha Perumal and Venkataramayya v. Venkataramana in discussing the differing historical views on the rule.
